draft.title: Who is a consumer
card: Consumer
A person who buys goods or services for personal or household use. Goods are things such as a phone. Services are things such as a haircut.
Purpose
What matters is why the item is bought. The same item can be bought for personal use or for running a business.
Imbalance
Sellers usually know more about the product and hold more power in a sale than the buyer does. A buyer may not be able to spot a fault or judge a claim.
Protection
Consumer law exists to reduce this imbalance. It sets rules for how sellers must treat the people who buy from them.
draft.remember: A consumer buys for personal or household use, and the law protects them because sellers usually have more power and information.

a.q: Why does consumer law protect people who buy goods and services?
opts: Sellers usually have more power and information
Consumers always know more than sellers do
Sellers are not allowed to make a profit
Consumers must be able to buy any product they want
a.why: Sellers usually know more about what they sell and hold more power in the sale, so the law steps in to reduce that imbalance. It does not say consumers know more, and it does not stop sellers making a profit.
a.clue: Think about who knows more about the product.

b.q: Priya buys a laptop from a shop in Parramatta. Which situation would make her a consumer in this purchase?
opts: She buys it for her own study at home
She buys it to use in her law firm
She buys ten to resell to customers
She buys it for her employer's office
b.why: A consumer buys for personal or household use, and study at home fits that. Buying for a firm, for resale or for an employer is a business purpose. The item is the same, but the reason for buying is different.
b.clue: Look at why she is buying, not what she is buying.

a.best: Sellers usually have more power and information

b.best: She buys it for her own study at home
also_right: She buys it to use in her law firm

problems.detail: The card says 'What matters is why the item is bought.' Under the Australian Consumer Law (s 3), a person is also a consumer if the goods cost $100,000 or less, or are of a kind ordinarily bought for personal, domestic or household use, whatever the purpose. Buying for resale or for use in manufacturing is excluded. So purpose is not the only test, and the card teaches HSC students a false version of the legal definition.

A laptop is ordinarily bought for personal use and costs well under $100,000. Under the ACL, Priya buying one for her law firm would still be a consumer, so that option is defensible as right. The why's claim that buying 'for a firm' or 'for an employer' is a business purpose that rules out consumer status is wrong under Australian law. Only the resale option is clearly excluded.

check.summary: The card and question b say consumer status depends only on why goods are bought. Under the Australian Consumer Law, goods costing $100,000 or less, or goods ordinarily bought for personal use, count regardless of purpose, so the law-firm laptop option in b is also legally right. Question a is fine.

proposal.title: Who is a consumer
card: Consumer
A person who buys goods or services, usually for personal or household use. Goods are things such as a phone. Services are things such as a haircut.
Legal test
Under the Australian Consumer Law, a buyer is also a consumer if the price is under a set limit, or the item is a kind usually bought for personal use. This holds even if it is bought for work.
Not a consumer
A person who buys goods to resell them, or to use up or transform in making other goods, is not a consumer of those goods.
Imbalance
Sellers usually know more about the product and hold more power in a sale. Consumer law exists to reduce this imbalance and sets rules for how sellers treat buyers.
proposal.remember: Buying to resell or to make other goods is excluded. The law protects consumers because sellers usually hold more power and information.

a.q: Why does consumer law protect people who buy goods and services?
opts: Sellers usually have more power and information
Consumers always know more than sellers do
Sellers are not allowed to make a profit
Consumers must be able to buy any product they want
a.why: Sellers usually know more about what they sell and hold more power in the sale, so the law steps in to reduce that imbalance. It does not say consumers know more, and it does not stop sellers making a profit.
a.clue: Think about who knows more about the product.

b.q: Priya buys laptops from a shop in Parramatta. Laptops are a kind of item usually bought for personal use. In which situation is she not a consumer?
opts: She buys ten to resell in her shop
She buys one for study at home
She buys one to use in her law firm
She buys one for her employer's office
b.why: Buying goods to resell them is excluded, so Priya is not a consumer of those ten laptops. Buying one for her law firm is tempting, but a laptop is a kind of item usually bought for personal use, so she is still a consumer.
b.clue: Which purchase is she planning to sell on to others?
